answer: Six registries by three columns. Cryptographic integrity hashes and marketplace-as-CA signatures are published, machine-readable at install, and (for npm ECDSA, PyPI file hashes, crates.io cksum, VS Code repository signing, Chrome store signing) applied when the registry accepts a package. OpenSSF OIDC Trusted Publishing is implemented by npm, PyPI, and crates.io; those three rows collapse to one independent signal (collapsed_shared_primitive_signals=2). OIDC is opt-in, so it is not a registry-wide publish gate. This program's marketplace surface has a generator provenance header (column a and a local slice of column b) and no publish-time identity or signature gate. The missing column is (c) enforced_at_publish. SUCCESS:RES-0047 in the receipt AND a six-registry three-column matrix with a stated count of collapsed shared-primitive signals.

collapse.rule: Independence is asserted, not assumed: rows that share shared_primitive_id count as one signal. collapsed_shared_primitive_signals is sum(len(group)-1) over groups with a shared primitive id.

evidence.claim: npm publishes ECDSA registry signatures that are machine-readable at install and applied on publish.
evidence.independence: API keys endpoint and a packument are different resources; they share the npm registry operator, not a second vendor.

evidence.claim: npm Trusted Publishing is OpenSSF OIDC; provenance appears as packument dist.attestations when present, and is not a mandatory publish gate.
evidence.independence: Packument attestations URL vs official npm docs. Same operator; second rail is documentation not a second registry.

evidence.claim: PyPI simple index publishes per-file SHA-256 fragments consumed at install.
evidence.independence: HTML simple API vs PEP 740 prose. Hash fragments predate PEP 740; the PEP is the attestation spec, used here only as the second rail for index-hosted integrity metadata.

evidence.claim: PyPI Trusted Publishing + PEP 740 attestations share the OIDC/Sigstore identity primitive; Integrity API returns attestation_bundles for requests 2.34.2.
evidence.independence: Integrity API JSON vs Trusted Publishers docs. Attestation certificate names sigstore.dev; docs name OIDC Trusted Publishers as the identity source.

evidence.claim: crates.io sparse index publishes cksum; cargo verifies it at install.
evidence.independence: Live index bytes vs RFC. RFC out-of-scope sentence is the control that cksum is not Sigstore provenance.

evidence.claim: crates.io implements OpenSSF-style OIDC trusted publishing (auth), without install-time provenance.
evidence.independence: Rust blog (announcement) vs RFC 3691 (spec). Same project, different document classes. The advertised docs URL 404'd with 0 bytes — that negative fetch is recorded, not silently skipped. Two prose rails, so this claim is not graded E1.

evidence.claim: Visual Studio Marketplace signs all extensions at publish; VS Code verifies at install.
evidence.independence: Two Microsoft doc pages (marketplace vs runtime-security). Same vendor; mechanically different URLs. No third-party API probe of a VSIX signature was run from this worktree.

evidence.claim: JetBrains Marketplace documents dual signing (author then Marketplace CA) with IDE verification; author signature absence is a warning.
evidence.independence: SDK docs (current) vs JetBrains Platform blog (2020-09). Same vendor, different URLs and dates. No live IDE signature verification was run.

evidence.claim: Chrome Web Store Google-signs every extension; verified uploads are an opt-in author-key check at upload, then the store re-signs.
evidence.independence: Chrome Developers blog (2025-05-07) vs publish docs. Same vendor, different URLs.

evidence.claim: npm, PyPI, and crates.io Trusted Publishing share one OpenSSF OIDC primitive; Homebrew bottle attestations share Sigstore/OIDC identity but Homebrew is outside the six.
evidence.independence: OpenSSF WG spec vs Homebrew docs. Homebrew is corroboration of the primitive, not a seventh matrix registry.

fetch_window.note: HTTP 404 on crates.io/docs/trusted-publishing is recorded. PyPI docs.pypi.org/attestations/security-model/ returned 429 on an earlier fetch; attestations intro and PEP 740 were used instead.

signals.caveat: The registry signs name@version:integrity with ecdsa-sha2-nistp256. This attests registry receipt of those bytes, not that the publisher was a specific CI identity. PGP signatures were deprecated 2023-04-25.
signals.name: ECDSA packument registry signatures

signals.caveat: OpenSSF Trusted Publishers via OIDC; provenance is generated by default on GitHub Actions / GitLab public publishes and can be disabled. Token publishes remain possible unless the package opts into 'disallow tokens'. Not a registry-wide publish gate.
signals.name: OIDC trusted publishing + automatic Sigstore provenance

signals.caveat: Every listed artifact URL carries #sha256=... pip/uv consume it. This is content addressing, not publisher identity.
signals.name: Simple-index file SHA-256 fragment

signals.caveat: If attestations are uploaded, the index MUST reject unverifiable ones (PEP 740). Uploading attestations is not required on every publish. Trusted Publishing is opt-in. pip does not verify attestations by default.
signals.name: OIDC trusted publishing + PEP 740 Sigstore attestations

signals.caveat: cargo verifies cksum of the downloaded .crate. This is integrity of the tarball against the index, not a publisher identity signature. RFC 3691 explicitly out-of-scopes Sigstore provenance.
signals.name: Sparse-index crate checksum

signals.caveat: Shipped per RFC 3691 / 2025-07-11 rust blog. OIDC authenticates publish; it does not attach a Sigstore attestation cargo can verify. First crate version must still be published manually. https://crates.io/docs/trusted-publishing returned HTTP 404 with empty body from this worktree on 2026-08-24 (advertised URL is JS SPA or moved); prose rail is the rust blog + RFC.
signals.name: OIDC trusted publishing (token exchange)

signals.caveat: Microsoft signs every extension at publish. VS Code verifies at install (extensions.verifySignature). This is marketplace-as-CA, not author identity and not OpenSSF OIDC.
signals.name: Marketplace repository signing of every VSIX

signals.caveat: Display-only trust badge. Domain proof is not a package signature. Unverified publishers can still publish.
signals.name: Verified publisher badge (DNS TXT + 6-month standing)

signals.caveat: Marketplace re-signs with JetBrains CA; IDEs verify that chain. Missing author signature produces an install warning, not a documented hard publish reject. Do not treat the warning as enforcement.
signals.name: Author signature plus JetBrains Marketplace CA re-sign

signals.caveat: Chrome Web Store signs packages with a Google-managed key. Anyone with Developer Dashboard access can upload a payload that then gets that signature. Review is a separate human process, not this crypto signal.
signals.name: Google store signing of every CRX

signals.caveat: Since 2025-05-07 a publisher may register an RSA public key; later unsigned uploads are rejected. Default remains Google-only signing. The author key is not the key Chrome verifies at install — the store re-packs with the existing private key so the extension ID is stable.
signals.name: Opt-in author-key verified uploads

program_missing_column_rationale: Column (c) is absent: there is no registry that refuses an unsigned, unattested, or non-OIDC publish of a markdown/script plugin. A2 TAMPERED detection is regenerate-vs-bytes after generation, not a publish-time trust gate. Column (b) for cryptographic attestations is also absent; do not read the A2 _generated header as Sigstore or marketplace-CA verification.
question: Across npm, PyPI, crates.io, the VS Code Marketplace, JetBrains and the Chrome Web Store, which trust signals are (a) published, (b) machine-readable at install time, and (c) enforced at publish time - and which of the three columns is the one this program is missing?

reviewer.anti_adoption_2: 05-ECO forbids a second same-vendor reviewer on the same input. Reviewer A sees only language-registry captures; reviewer B sees only app-store captures. The OIDC collapse claim is checked by A from npm/PyPI/crates sources; B does not re-judge those files.

reviewers.notes: Checked ECDSA keys/packument, PyPI simple+integrity, crates index cksum, and the OIDC three-row collapse.
Checked VS Code repository signing, JetBrains dual-sign docs, Chrome store signing and verified-uploads. Did not read npm/PyPI/crates captures.

sentinel: SUCCESS:RES-0047 in the receipt AND a six-registry three-column matrix with a stated count of collapsed shared-primitive signals

homebrew_out_of_scope.role: corroborating third-or-fourth implementation of OIDC/Sigstore identity

shared_primitive_rule.statement: Sources sharing one upstream primitive count as ONE signal. Catalog example: npm/PyPI/Homebrew signing share one OIDC primitive. Homebrew is outside the six; crates.io now implements the same OpenSSF OIDC Trusted Publishers primitive (RFC 3691). npm provenance and PyPI PEP 740 attestations are the artifact-binding half of that same identity primitive, not a second independent signal.

strongest_surviving_counterargument: A reader could call column (b) the missing one, because this program has no install-time signature verifier. That is true for cryptographic attestations. The question asks for the one column; (c) is the cleaner answer because even the metadata that exists is not gated at publish, while (a) is satisfied by listings and A2 headers. Treating A2 regenerate-as-restore as publish enforcement would overclaim.

tests.name: Six-registry three-column matrix plus live capture facts
Independent shared-primitive collapse recount plus local missing-column scan

this_program.note: command-center/phase3/A2/DESIGN.json is absent on this worktree (ARC-0010 catalog output). Local scan uses the generated marketplace fixture plus the live typed A2 registry at command-center/p2-wave/probes/ARC-0010/registry.json. Those files carry a generator provenance header and no OIDC/Sigstore/trusted-publisher fields. Absence of DESIGN.json is not treated as a publish-time identity gate.

title: Comparative teardown: which trust signals each mature package registry actually exposes
